planting.note: Grow in bright light to full sun in an extremely fast-draining, mineral succulent mix; withhold all water through the winter dormant split and resume only after the old leaf pair has fully desiccated.

directions: This is one of the largest-bodied Lithops species in cultivation, with broad rusty-brown to reddish-tan paired leaves marked by darker branching channels and islands that mimic weathered quartzite pebbles. New leaf pairs emerge each spring and consume the old pair entirely, so the plant appears to split and shed rather than grow taller. Never water while the previous leaf pair is still plump, since the body has no way to lose that excess moisture and will rupture or rot. Feed sparingly if at all, and expect a single daisy-like yellow flower to emerge from the leaf fissure in mid to late autumn.

planting.note: Grow in bright light to full sun in an extremely fast-draining, mineral succulent mix; keep completely dry through the winter rest and let the outer skin fully shrivel before the first watering of the season.

directions: The paired leaf bodies of this species are a dull tawny-copper to grayish-brown with a finely wrinkled, almost suede-like surface texture that sets it apart from the smoother-faced Lithops species. A network of faint darker dots and shallow surface dimples further breaks up its outline against gravel mulch. Because the body sits nearly flush with the soil line, extra care is needed to keep grit from packing into the leaf fissure where rot can start unnoticed. A solitary yellow flower opens in the afternoon in autumn, and the annual leaf-pair exchange should never be watered along until the spent leaves are paper-dry.

planting.note: Grow in bright light to full sun in an extremely fast-draining, mineral succulent mix; this is one of the easiest and fastest-maturing Lithops for beginners, but still needs a bone-dry winter dormancy.

directions: Widely regarded as the most weather- and beginner-tolerant Lithops in cultivation, this species forms small clustering groups of grayish-tan to pale khaki leaf pairs with a scattering of darker reddish-brown surface markings resembling pitted stone. It reliably offsets into multi-headed clumps faster than most other species, making it a common gateway plant for new mesemb growers. A bright yellow flower with a white throat opens on sunny autumn afternoons and closes each evening for several days running. Resist the urge to water the moment new leaves are visible in the fissure; wait until the old pair is fully spent and dry to avoid splitting the body.

planting.note: Grow in bright light to full sun in an extremely fast-draining, mineral succulent mix; native to saline pan margins, it tolerates mildly mineral-heavy water better than most Lithops but still demands a fully dry dormant season.

directions: Named for its native habitat on saline flats near South African salt pans, this species has smooth gray-green to bluish leaf tops etched with faint translucent windows and darker olive channels. It clumps readily into tight multi-headed mats over a few seasons, forming a low mounded colony that reads as a scatter of rounded pebbles. Its slightly more forgiving tolerance of mineral buildup in the soil makes it a practical choice where tap water is hard, though drainage must still be immaculate. A crisp white to pale yellow daisy-like flower appears in early autumn, and watering should stay suspended until the newest leaf pair has fully taken over from the old one.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America (CSSA)

planting.note: Grow in bright light with some protection from the hottest midday sun, in an extremely fast-draining mineral mix; this winter-grower goes fully dormant and must stay bone-dry through summer heat.

directions: This clumping species forms dense mounds of small, fused, grayish-green bilobed bodies dusted with a fine waxy bloom that give a colony the look of a cluster of smooth river pebbles. Unlike the summer-dormant Lithops, this Conophytum is a winter grower, actively rooting and flowering from autumn through spring before shutting down completely for the hot summer months. Fragrant magenta-pink flowers open in the late afternoon in fall, often covering the whole clump at once and perfuming the area nearby. Every drop of water must be withheld from late spring through summer while the outer skin of each body dries to a papery sheath protecting the dormant plant beneath.

planting.note: Grow in bright light with some protection from the hottest midday sun, in an extremely fast-draining mineral mix; like other winter-growing Conophytum, it must be kept fully dry during its summer dormancy.

directions: This species forms tight cushions of small, rounded, blue-green to grayish bodies patterned with faint darker dots and a slightly rough, dull-textured surface distinct from the glossier finish of related species. Colonies slowly widen into low domed mats as older heads split into two or three new bodies each growing season. Small pink to purple daisy-like flowers appear in the fall, usually opening only in bright sunlight and closing again by evening. Because this species is especially prone to rot if watered while the old skin is still intact, always wait for the papery outer layer to fully split and dry before resuming any water in early autumn.

planting.note: Grow in bright light to full sun in an extremely fast-draining, mineral succulent mix; suspend watering entirely during the summer dormancy that follows spring flowering to avoid rot.

directions: A smaller-bodied relative of split rock, this species forms compact clusters of thick, rounded gray-green leaf pairs covered in fine darker speckles that mimic granite pebbles scattered on desert soil. Unlike its larger cousin, it clumps more readily, producing new heads at the base each year to form a tight, low colony over time. Large daisy-like flowers in yellow or coppery-orange open on sunny afternoons in late summer or early fall, often nearly as wide as the leaf body itself. Water only sparingly and only when the leaves show visible softening or wrinkling, since this genus stores enough moisture in its thick leaves to go many weeks without irrigation even in active growth.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America (CSSA)
